paragraphs: Overall credibility of the results is unknown, so the results must not be described as converged or trustworthy. In static step s1, the reaction balance check passed: the applied load is balanced by the support reactions.

The mesh quality check for s1 is unknown. Second-order elements on curved surfaces became too distorted after order elevation, so straight-edge second-order elements were used and the curved surfaces are approximated by chords. Stresses near curved surfaces may therefore deviate noticeably.

The maximum von Mises stress, excluding the constrained faces, is {{s1.vm_max_mpa}}, and the maximum displacement is {{s1.u_max_mm}}. The material yield strength is {{s1.strength_mpa}}. These values are reported for reference only and are not a pass/fail assessment.

The mesh convergence checks passed for both quantities. Maximum stress over the three mesh levels is {{s1.conv2.level0}}, {{s1.conv2.level1}} and {{s1.conv2.level2}}, which oscillates within the tolerance. Maximum displacement is {{s1.conv3.level0}}, {{s1.conv3.level1}} and {{s1.conv3.level2}}, with very small differences between levels. This does not remove the unknown mesh quality status.
No safety factor is given, because the credibility checks did not pass (the conclusion is unknown).

In modal step m1, the first four natural frequencies are {{m1.f1_hz}}, {{m1.f2_hz}}, {{m1.f3_hz}} and {{m1.f4_hz}}. The equivalent rotational speeds are {{m1.f1_rpm}}, {{m1.f2_rpm}}, {{m1.f3_rpm}} and {{m1.f4_rpm}}. The first two modes are very close to each other.

Limitations: the model is linear elastic with small deformation, with no contact, residual stress or surface hardening. Stresses near constrained and loaded faces come from idealized boundary conditions and were excluded from the maximum. Stresses at sharp corners grow with mesh refinement (theoretical singularity) and should not be used directly for design. Only the part's own mass and stiffness are included, so attached masses are ignored. Supports are ideal, so real bearing stiffness would lower the frequencies.
suggestions: Refine the mesh on the curved surfaces so that there are several element layers across them, then rerun to clear the mesh quality check.
Have an engineer review the stress results near curved surfaces, because the chord approximation may bias them.
Do not use the corner stresses at sharp corners directly; add a realistic fillet radius or evaluate by a method that avoids the singularity.
Add the mass of attached components to the modal model to check how the natural frequencies shift.
Provide actual bearing stiffness data and update the support model, since ideal supports overestimate the frequencies.
Have an engineer check the operating speed range against the listed natural frequencies, particularly the closely spaced first two modes.
